articles.title: Ntelesimi - The Household Demon
articles.excerpt: Tradition about the spirit 'ntelesimi' with Turkish-Arabic etymology and destructive behavior on winter nights.

content.value: The tradition recorded by S. Skipis (1908) analyzes the name 'ntelesimi,' which is of Turkish origin and derives from the word 'telesim,' which in turn comes from the Arabic 'tilisim' and is connected to the Greek 'telesma.' In this tradition, the term 'ntelesimi' appears to refer to a household demon or spirit that dwells in the basement areas, in damp and deep parts of the house, and is bound throughout the entire year.

However, on winter nights, this spirit manages to break free of its bonds and causes great upheaval and destruction in the house's garden. The description of this tradition seems to follow the classic tradition of haunted houses,
Studies on the Life and Language of the Greek People, N. G. Politis - Traditions Part B 1904 - p. 1102

articles.title: The Saganakia of Xylokastro
articles.author: Νικόλαος Γ. Πολίτης
articles.excerpt: Folk belief about the underworld powers of the saganakia and the magic of the curse

content.value: When the Saganakia pass by, they move in processions and voices and commotion are heard, made by the demons inside. And if someone happens to curse another person at that moment, the curse takes hold.

So, once, a mother was cursing her child; and a wicked neighbor, shortly after, when Saganakia were passing with sprites inside, called out to her immediately: 'Neighbor, neighbor, if you want to curse your child now — there are processions passing and your curse will take hold!' 'Ha, may your own eyes fall out instead — I would never curse my own child!' the mother replied, and the wicked neighbor's eyes fell out immediately at that very moment.

articles.title: The Demonic Council - Sfakia
articles.author: Νικόλαος Γ. Πολίτης
articles.excerpt: Dramatic account of a supernatural encounter with a demonic council in the mountains of Sfakia

content.value: Once, a man told me a tale: two men had been out in the cold in the highest mountains, where wild ibex dwell. They sat one moonlit night at a mountain pass to hunt wild ibex.
And there they heard a great commotion, and they thought it must be people loading snow to take it to Chania.
And as they drew closer, they heard violins and lyres and music of all sorts, the likes of which they had never heard before. At that they realized these were not people, but a demonic council.

And they watched them pass close by where they were sitting, wearing garments of all kinds, some with dapple-gray horses, others with varied attire, and it was clear there were women and men, on foot and on horseback — a great multitude.
And the men were white as doves, and the women crimson and beautiful, like the rays of the sun. They also saw them carrying something, as one carries a dead man.
They then decided to fire a shot at them as they passed in front. And there was a song to be heard, with the words: 'A bride we go to fetch, a noble bride, a lone bride from Krimismeno.'

And they decided and fired a shot. At that, the ones in front called out with a single voice: 'What is that?' And the ones behind answered: 'You have killed our bridegroom! You have killed our bridegroom!' And they wept and cried out and fled.

articles.title: The Vrachnas in Crete
articles.author: Μανούσος Ι. Κόρακας & Νικόλαος Πολίτης
articles.excerpt: Ethnographic study of the Vrachnas, the demonic creature that causes nightmares in Sfakia, Crete. The etymology of the name, the experiences of sufferers, and historical references from Byzantium to the Cypriot dialect are examined.

content.value: The Vrachnas. Many beliefs exist in Sfakia, Crete regarding the nightmare and the etymology of the name Vrachnas. The Vrachnas is not a devil but a demonic creature that seizes people in light sleep. Many who suffer from it say that before they feel it on their chest, they hear its footsteps as it enters the room where they are sleeping and see it in the shape of a cat. If someone manages to get up beforehand, sensing the evil that approaches, they are rid of it; otherwise they must pray for it to leave. When someone experiences the Vrachnas and it overcomes them, they feel that its power is so great that they cannot cry out.

Regarding the etymology of the Cretan name for the nightmare, I understand it is called this because 'it takes away the voice and makes a person become hoarse.' The author also observes that in the exorcisms of St. Basil the Great it is mentioned that 'a demon schemed in deep sleep.' It is not the same interpretation, since St. Basil the Great, with the meaning of deep sleep, was most likely referring to spiritual sleep, and with the word demon was referring to temptation.

The word 'vrachnas' is also mentioned by Korais (Atakt. T. D. p. 47) but he notes that the correct spelling is 'varychnas' on account of the weight it produces. From Byzantine times it survives as 'vrachnas,' 'svrachnas,' or 'vrafnas.'
An even older surviving name from the Cypriot dialect is called 'varypnan' or 'garypnan,' meaning the nightmare.
Sakellarios surmises that in Cypriot the word is compound, derived from 'varys' (heavy) and 'pnoe' (breath).

articles.title: The Koloupanas of Nafpaktia
articles.author: Δημ Λουκόπουλος
articles.excerpt: Folkloric record of the Koloupanas, a demonic creature that kills sheep and appears as a dog or goat. It appeared at night in Oxia, Nafpaktia (modern-day Lefka). Local names include Kolopani and Iskios.

content.value: The Kouloupaṇas is a sprite (demon). It goes and impregnates sheep, and they die. And it climbs the barren ground that grows no trees toward Oxia (the area). It resembles a dog, bleats sometimes like a sheep, sometimes like a goat. It came out at night.
Author's note: At the time he was telling me the story, he asked me why I wanted to learn these things.
The Kouloupaṇas, or at other times Iskios, in Mikri Paloukova (modern-day Lefka), Nafpaktia, a mountain village built at the foothills of Oxia, is also known as Kolopanis.

articles.title: The Exorcism of the Herd in Nigrita
articles.author: George Frederick Abbott
articles.excerpt: Anthropological record of a livestock exorcism ceremony in Nigrita, Serres. The priest, holding the hand of Saint Dionysios, blessed the sick cattle one by one by name, while the inhabitants treated the ritual with both seriousness and humor.

image.alt: Traditional church in Nigrita, site of the Animal Blessing

content.value: In Nigrita I had the opportunity to witness a ceremony of this kind — an Animal Blessing. The cattle of the area had been struck by a disease, which, as was natural, was attributed to the workings of the Evil One. So the inhabitants decided to perform an exorcism.

On Saturday evening, the town crier (Turkish: dellal) announced that the following morning the sick animals were to be led to the churchyard. The next day, many cattle of every age and color, male and female, gathered in the church courtyard, awaiting the special ceremony that would be performed for their benefit.

When the regular Sunday service was over, the priest came outside and, holding before him the hand of Saint Dionysios, the patron saint of the village, read the prescribed prayer, calling each ox, cow, and calf by name and beseeching God's mercy for each one individually.

When he mentioned names such as 'Mavroula,' 'Kokkinoula,' 'Pitsiloti,' 'Moraïtissa,' and others, the priest found it difficult to restrain his laughter at the comical aspect of the ceremony — a sentiment shared with a smile by some of the farmers. Nevertheless, though they saw the comic element, they took the blessing of their livestock very seriously and did not interrupt the ceremony.

articles.title: The Anemikes - Dasyllio, Grevena
articles.author: Δημ. Λουκόπουλος
articles.excerpt: Traditional beliefs about the Anemikes (Spring demons) in Dasyllio, Grevena, who cause harm during the first ten days of March. Protective measures and treatment for those afflicted are described.

content.value: The Anemikes are spring demons (especially of the month of March); they are invisible but cause harm. During the first ten days of March, their malign influence is particularly noticeable and for this reason protective measures must be taken. Women must not wash their hair, must not sleep in the afternoon, must not urinate in places where ash has been thrown.

If someone falls asleep outdoors and wakes up afflicted, they must smear the ground with honey, gather dry herbs and other objects from that spot and take them home to burn in the fireplace. The smoke produced by the burning must come into contact with them (they must be fumigated) so as to be rid of the affliction.

articles.title: The Devil, the Fires and the Zouzoula - Vrysika, Evros
articles.author: Ιωάννης Γουρίδης
articles.excerpt: Folk narratives about evil spirits (zouzoula) and diabolical fires in Vrysika, Evros, with two specific stories.

content.value: The devil is the leader of all evil spirits.
His minions (zouzoula, stoicheia) are the evil sprites. The zouzoula would appear to people in the form of animals: a bear, cat, dog, etc., or as fire.
In a place where someone had been killed, a fire would appear.
Various stories exist about the zouzoula:
1) To the southwest of the village there is a large tree. The Altın-Karayatsi or Trouchola's Karagatsi. There a spirit would appear. A flame would emerge and illuminate gold coins.

2) At the katsiféla, east of the village, above the road from Kyani to Vrysika, a spirit would appear — a sow with her piglets. These would take hold of, drag away, the nocturnal traveler and carry him to the river to drown him.

articles.title: The Zouzoulia of Didymoteicho
articles.author: Α. Τσακίρη
articles.excerpt: Story of a farmer who encountered zouzoulia at a fountain and was protected by heeding his grandmother's advice.

content.value: Once, a man set off with his cart to go to a neighboring village. On his way, he came to a fountain.

At that fountain he saw a beautiful dance, led by strapping men dressed as evzones and women dressed in Souliote attire. When the villager reached the fountain, they stopped him and all those people who were dancing leaped onto his cart.

The villager struck his animals, but they would not move. He struck them, struck them again, the animals would not move. Then the villager remembered his grandmother's words: 'Stop at the fountain and wait for the roosters to crow.'
As soon as the roosters crowed, those zouzoulia departed without harming the villager. The villager, happy that nothing had happened to him, headed home.

articles.title: The Devils at the Mill - Western Macedonia
articles.author: Φώτης Δημ. Παπανικολάου
articles.excerpt: Tale about a mill-builder who outwits devils using their own secret, according to the tradition of Western Macedonia.

content.value: Once, a man was building a mill inside a pit. By day he built it, and at night the devils would come and tear it down. The man said: 'I'll go and keep watch tonight, to see who it is that's wrecking my mill!' He went and hid nearby.

When night fell, the devils started coming. They gathered and sat down, and the chief devil was laughing and saying: 'Ha, look at the poor wretch, what he's going through! He builds and we wreck! Let's see how long this work will hold!'
Hmm! said a little devil: 'Well, he doesn't know the remedy to throw it — otherwise we couldn't come here and wreck his mill!'
'And what is that remedy?' the chief devil burst out and said.

'Why,' said the little devil, 'he should go to a place where roosters cannot be heard, find a wild cherry tree, cut it down, take a piece of its wood, place it on the holy altar table, and leave it there for forty days! Then take it and place it here where he's building the mill. That will keep us devils away from coming and wrecking his mill!'

The devils tore down the mill again and, prancing and dancing, went away. He got up, went to a place where no roosters could be heard, found a wild cherry tree, cut it down and did what he had heard from the devil. That was it! The devils never set foot at the mill again!

articles.title: Goat's Wool and the Devils - Petralona, Olympia
articles.excerpt: A folk belief from Petralona, Olympia: a dying person covered with a saïsma (goat's wool coverlet) cannot pass away easily, because goat's wool has dealings with the Devil.

content.value: A person in their final moments of life does not pass away easily if they are covered with a saïsma [a coverlet made of goat's wool], because the wool from which it is made comes from the goat, which has dealings with the Devil.

articles.title: Demonic Gathering at Nerosyrtis, Amvrakia - Trichonia
articles.excerpt: A testimony from Nerosyrtis, Aetolia-Acarnania: near the small chapel on the rock, pebbles fall upon the rock and onto the plane trees day and night. The locals attribute this to a demonic gathering.

content.value: Near the small chapel beyond the rock, pebbles fall from above the rock, onto the plane trees. Whether you pass very late at night or even during the day, you can hear pebbles falling. There must be a demonic gathering there.
